memoryText: And who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Esther 4:14 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This question was asked by an older cousin to a frightened young queen. It is a question, not a command, and that is part of its power.

“Who knows.” Mordecai does not claim certainty. He cannot see the future. He is asking Esther to consider a possibility. God’s purposes are often hidden, and we act without a guarantee. Faith lives in the space between what we know and what we hope.

“Whether you have not come to the kingdom.” Esther did not choose to be queen. She was taken to the palace by force, hidden her identity, and lived in a gilded cage. Everything that happened to her could have looked like loss. Mordecai invites her to see a different story. Her position was not an accident.

“For such a time as this.” This is a call to the present. Esther was not asked to be queen in some other age. She was asked to act now. Our callings are tied to particular moments: this family, this job, this friendship, this crisis. We do not choose the time, but we are asked to meet it.

The verse comes just after a sobering warning. If she keeps silent, deliverance will come from another place. God does not need us. But he invites us. The honor is in being used.

Keep this verse near when you face a decision that is uncomfortable. You are where you are for a reason. Ask God what he wants to do through you.
weekInReview: This week you finished Nehemiah and read the book of Esther. You saw the wall dedicated with two choirs and a sound of joy heard far away, and you saw how quickly the people slipped back into their old ways. Nehemiah ended with a prayer: “Remember me, O my God, for good.” Then you moved to Persia and read the story of Esther, in which God’s name never appears and his hand is everywhere. You watched a queen risk her life, a sleepless king, a proud man hanged on his own gallows, and a day of sorrow turned into gladness. In Psalm 145, you praised the God who is near to all who call on him. In Psalms 149 and 150, you sang a new song and let everything that has breath praise the LORD.
reflectionQuestions: Esther was asked to risk her position for others. What position, gift, or influence has God given you that could be used for someone else?
The book of Esther never names God, yet his work is visible. Where do you see his hidden hand in your own story?
Both Nehemiah and Esther point to a people who still need a better deliverer. How does Jesus fulfill what these books long for?
prayerPrompts: Ask God to give you courage and wisdom for the season you are in.
Thank him for his hidden hand and nearness.
